faq.q: What is an AI clip for YouTube Shorts ads?
faq.a: A tall product video made from your photo or your product link, with an [AI actor](/ai-video-generation/ai-actors) and a voice you can edit. It is not a real customer review.

faq.q: Can I customize the script, actor, and visuals?
faq.a: Yes. Rewrite the script, swap the actor, change the voice, and adjust the scene before you download.

faq.q: What does a Short cost in credits?
faq.a: A clip costs 24, 40, 60 or 120 credits for 6, 10, 15 or 30 seconds. The price shows before you start. If a file fails, those credits return on their own. There is no free plan.

faq.q: Are AI clips allowed in YouTube ads?
faq.a: Follow Google's current ad-review and disclosure rules on the day you publish. We do not submit the ad, and we do not guarantee approval. Do not present a generated actor as a real customer.

faq.q: How should I treat the actors and voices?
faq.a: They are generated presenters, not people you hired. You can change the tone and the language. Do not claim a shopper will mistake them for a customer.

faq.q: Does a Short start from a product link?
faq.a: Yes. Paste a product page link, or upload a photo. A 16:9 in-stream ad is a separate wide file. Do not crop a wide ad and use it as a Short.
We do not promise a longer watch. You can try another opening, actor, or script, and you choose which file to publish.
Use [social media ad sizes](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform) before you export, and keep the product clear of the player controls.

reviews.h2: How shops use YouTube Shorts ads
reviews.lead: A few ways shops open a Short from one product.

items.d: A kitchen shop uses a pan photo for one cook motion, with the handle kept visible.
A beauty shop uses a gloss photo for a swatch, with the tube still in frame.
An electronics shop uses an earbud case photo for an open-case hold.
A drink seller uses a can photo for a short pour, with the label facing the camera.
A home shop uses a lamp photo for a switch-on, so the shade shape is easy to see.
A fitness shop uses a mat photo for an unroll, so the length is easy to see.
An apparel shop uses a jacket photo for one zip, with the collar kept in frame.
A pet shop uses a brush photo for a short grooming pass so the size is easy to see.
A jewelry shop uses a necklace photo for a clasp close-up, with the chain fully visible.
An outdoor shop uses a bottle photo for a sip, so the logo stays easy to read.
